A piecewise function is continuous at the join when the two pieces **agree** there.
**Step 1 — identify the join.** The definition changes at **x = 5**:
f(x) = 3x − 8 for x ≤ 5
f(x) = 2k for x > 5
**Step 2 — write the value at x = 5 and the left-hand limit.** The first branch covers
x = 5 itself, so
f(5) = 3(5) − 8 = 15 − 8 = **7**
and approaching from the left gives the same, since 3x − 8 is continuous:
lim(x→5⁻) f(x) = **7**
**Step 3 — write the right-hand limit.** For x > 5 the function is the **constant** 2k, so
lim(x→5⁺) f(x) = **2k**
**Step 4 — set them equal**, which is what continuity at x = 5 requires:
2k = 7
**k = 7/2** ✓
**Check.** With k = 7/2 the function is
f(x) = 3x − 8 for x ≤ 5, and 3·5 − 8 = 7 for x > 5
so the graph is a straight line of gradient 3 that stops at (5, 7) and continues as a
horizontal line at height 7 — no jump at the join ✓ (There is a **corner** there, so f is
continuous but not differentiable at 5 — continuity is all the question asks.)
**The three conditions for continuity at a point**, all satisfied here:
**f(5) exists** — it is 7 ✓
**lim(x→5) f(x) exists** — both one-sided limits are 7 ✓
**the two agree** ✓
**Why the fractions with 7 in the denominator are offered.** Options 2/7, 3/7 and 4/7 all
invert the fraction or mis-solve 2k = 7. The equation is 2k = 7, so k = 7 **divided by** 2,
giving **7/2 = 3·5** — a number greater than 1, while all three distractors are less
than 1. Noticing that 2k must equal 7 and so k must exceed 3 eliminates them at a glance.
∴ 7/2.

The **greatest integer function** [x] is a staircase: constant on each interval between
consecutive integers, and **jumping** at every integer.
**Step 1 — describe the discontinuities.** At an integer n,
lim(x→n⁻) [x] = **n − 1** (approaching from below, [x] still equals n − 1)
lim(x→n⁺) [x] = **n** (just above n, [x] has jumped to n)
The two one-sided limits differ by **1**, so the limit does not exist and [x] is
**discontinuous at every integer** ✓
**Step 2 — describe the continuities.** If a is **not** an integer, there is a whole
interval around a on which [x] is **constant**, equal to [a]. A function constant near a
point is certainly continuous there ✓ So [x] is **continuous at every non-integer**.
**Step 3 — test the options.**
**4** — an integer ✗ discontinuous
**−2** — an integer ✗ discontinuous
**1** — an integer ✗ discontinuous
**1·5** — **not** an integer ✓ continuous
**Step 4 — verify at x = 1·5.** Near 1·5, say on (1, 2), every x has [x] = **1**. So
lim(x→1·5) [x] = 1 and [1·5] = 1 ✓ The function is locally constant there, hence
continuous.
**And at x = 1, for contrast.**
lim(x→1⁻)[x] = **0** (values just below 1, such as 0·99, have [x] = 0)
lim(x→1⁺)[x] = **1**
f(1) = [1] = 1
The left limit disagrees, so there is a **jump discontinuity** at 1 ✗
**The shape of the graph.** It is a series of horizontal segments, each closed on the left
and open on the right:
… on [−1, 0) the value is −1; on [0, 1) it is 0; on [1, 2) it is 1; on [2, 3) it is 2 …
and the jumps occur exactly at the integers. Only three of the four options are integers,
so the answer stands out once the rule is known.
∴ 1·5.

then see what the square root produces on it.

9 − x² ≥ 0
x² ≤ 9
**−3 ≤ x ≤ 3**
**Step 2 — find what 9 − x² ranges over on that domain.** As x runs from −3 to 3, x² runs
over **[0, 9]**, so
9 − x² runs over **[0, 9]**
reaching **9** at x = 0 and **0** at x = ±3.
**Step 3 — take the square root.** The square root is increasing, so it maps [0, 9] onto
√0 to √9, that is
**[0, 3]** ✓

**closed at both ends**.

y² = 9 − x², that is **x² + y² = 9**

range is **[0, a]** — never negative, because the square-root symbol denotes the

Test the two properties separately — **one-one** (injective) and **onto** (surjective) —
for f : R → R with f(x) = x⁴.
**Step 1 — test one-one.** A function is one-one when different inputs give different
outputs. Here
f(1) = 1⁴ = **1** and f(−1) = (−1)⁴ = **1**
Two different inputs, 1 and −1, give the **same** output ✗
**f is not one-one.**
This happens for **every** non-zero x, since f(−x) = (−x)⁴ = x⁴ = f(x): the fourth power
destroys the sign, so the function is **even** and its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
No even function (other than a constant restricted suitably) can be one-one on a domain
symmetric about 0.
**Step 2 — test onto.** The codomain is **R**, so every real number must be attained. But
x⁴ ≥ 0 for every real x
so **no negative number** is ever an output. For instance there is no real x with
x⁴ = **−1** ✗
**f is not onto.** Its actual range is **[0, ∞)**, a proper subset of R.
**Step 3 — conclude.** f is **neither one-one nor onto** ✓
**Why the other options fail.**
**one-one and onto** ✗ — it is neither.
**one-one but not onto** ✗ — the surjectivity half is right, but injectivity fails, as
f(1) = f(−1) shows.
**may be one-one and onto** ✗ — there is nothing uncertain here; both properties are
definitively false.
**How restricting changes things.** The failures are both about the **sets** involved,
not the formula:
f : [0, ∞) → R is **one-one** (but still not onto)
f : R → [0, ∞) is **onto** (but still not one-one)
f : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) is a **bijection**, with inverse x^(1/4)
So "is x⁴ a bijection?" has no answer until the domain and codomain are stated — which is
exactly what the question is testing.
∴ f is neither one-one nor onto.

Each inverse trigonometric function is given a **principal branch** so that it is
single-valued, and for sec⁻¹ that branch is
**[0, π] − {π/2}** ✓
**Why [0, π] is the right interval.** sec x = 1/cos x, so sec⁻¹ is built on the same branch
as cos⁻¹, whose range is **[0, π]**. Indeed
sec⁻¹x = cos⁻¹(1/x)
and as 1/x runs over [−1, 1] \ {0}, cos⁻¹(1/x) runs over [0, π] without π/2.
**Why π/2 must be removed.** At x = π/2 the cosine is **zero**, so sec(π/2) = 1/0 is
undefined. The secant never takes any value there, so π/2 can never be the output of
sec⁻¹ ✗ It is a single point punched out of an otherwise closed interval.
**The matching domain.** |sec x| ≥ 1 always, so sec⁻¹ is defined only for
**|x| ≥ 1**, that is on (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞) — never for x strictly between −1 and 1.
**How the branch divides.**
for **x ≥ 1**, sec⁻¹x lies in **[0, π/2)** — for example sec⁻¹1 = 0 and sec⁻¹2 = π/3
for **x ≤ −1**, sec⁻¹x lies in **(π/2, π]** — for example sec⁻¹(−1) = π and
sec⁻¹(−2) = 2π/3
The two halves meet at π/2, which belongs to neither, and that is where the gap sits.
**Why the other options are wrong.**
**[−π/2, π/2]** ✗ — this is the range of **sin⁻¹** (and, open-ended, of tan⁻¹).
**(−π/2, π/2)** ✗ — the range of **tan⁻¹**.
**[0, π]** ✗ — the range of **cos⁻¹**, and it is right apart from the single missing point.
That near-miss is the whole question: sec⁻¹ shares cos⁻¹'s interval but **excludes π/2**.
**The full table, worth memorising.**
sin⁻¹: [−π/2, π/2] cos⁻¹: [0, π]
tan⁻¹: (−π/2, π/2) cot⁻¹: (0, π)
**sec⁻¹: [0, π] − {π/2}** cosec⁻¹: [−π/2, π/2] − {0}
Notice the pattern: each reciprocal function copies its partner's interval and removes the
one point where the partner vanishes.
∴ [0, π] − {π/2}.

Both properties must be tested, and a single counter-example settles each.
**Step 1 — test commutativity.** We need a ∗ b = b ∗ a for **all** a, b. Take a = 1, b = 2:
1 ∗ 2 = 1/(2 + 1) = **1/3**
2 ∗ 1 = 2/(1 + 1) = **1**
Different ✗ so ∗ is **not commutative**.
The asymmetry is visible in the formula itself: a appears in the **numerator** while b
appears in the **denominator**, so the two play quite different roles.
**Step 2 — test associativity.** We need (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c) for all a, b, c. Take
a = b = c = 1:
**left side:** 1 ∗ 1 = 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2, then (1/2) ∗ 1 = (1/2)/(1 + 1) = **1/4**
**right side:** 1 ∗ 1 = 1/2, then 1 ∗ (1/2) = 1/((1/2) + 1) = 1/(3/2) = **2/3**
1/4 ≠ 2/3 ✗ so ∗ is **not associative**.
**Step 3 — conclude.** ∗ is **neither associative nor commutative** ✓
**The general forms, for completeness.**
(a ∗ b) ∗ c = [a/(b + 1)]/(c + 1) = **a/[(b + 1)(c + 1)]**
a ∗ (b ∗ c) = a/[b/(c + 1) + 1] = **a(c + 1)/(b + c + 1)**
These agree only for very special values, not in general.
**Why −1 is excluded from the set.** The operation divides by **b + 1**, which vanishes
when b = −1. Removing −1 from R is what makes a ∗ b defined for every pair in the set —
the usual reason a single point is deleted in questions of this kind. (Strictly, the
operation is not quite closed either, since a ∗ b can equal −1; the question sets that
aside.)
**How to tackle such a question quickly.** Commutativity is checked by the simplest
unequal pair, usually 1 and 2; associativity by the simplest triple, usually 1, 1, 1. If
both fail, the answer is "neither" — and here the lopsided formula a/(b + 1) makes both
failures likely before any arithmetic is done.
∴ ∗ is neither associative nor commutative.

Two separate limits, each evaluated from the branch that applies near the point.
**The function.**
f(x) = x² − 1 for x ≥ 2
f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2
**Step 1 — the limit as x → 1.** The point 1 is **well inside** the region x < 2, so only
the second branch matters and the function is continuous there:
lim(x→1) f(x) = 1 + 1 = **2**
**Step 2 — the limit as x → 2.** Here 2 is the **join**, so both one-sided limits must be
checked.
**from the left** (x < 2, second branch):
lim(x→2⁻) f(x) = 2 + 1 = **3**
**from the right** (x ≥ 2, first branch):
lim(x→2⁺) f(x) = 2² − 1 = 4 − 1 = **3**
The two agree, so the limit **exists**:
lim(x→2) f(x) = **3**
(In fact f(2) = 3 as well, so f is **continuous** at the join — the pieces have been chosen
to meet.)
**Step 3 — add.**
2 + 3 = **5** ✓
**Why the second limit had to be checked from both sides.** At a point where the definition
changes, a limit exists only if the two branches approach the same value. Had the first
branch been, say, x² + 1, the right limit would be 5 against a left limit of 3, the limit
at 2 would not exist, and the question would have no answer. Checking both sides is not a
formality.
**Why the first limit did not.** At x = 1 there is no change of definition — the whole
neighbourhood (0, 2) uses x + 1 — so a single substitution suffices.
**Reading the distractors.** **3** is the second limit alone; **7** would come from using
x² − 1 at x = 1, giving 0, plus… no sensible route; **9** from using x² − 1 at both points,
0 + 3. The answer needs the **correct branch at each point**, and then the sum.
∴ 5.

x = tan θ collapses the inverse sine to a simple multiple of θ.
**Step 1 — substitute.** Let **x = tan θ**, so θ = tan⁻¹x. Then
2x/(1 + x²) = 2 tan θ/(1 + tan²θ) = 2 tan θ/sec²θ
= 2 (sin θ/cos θ) cos²θ
= 2 sin θ cos θ
= **sin 2θ**
**Step 2 — apply the inverse sine.**
f(x) = sin⁻¹(sin 2θ) = **2θ = 2 tan⁻¹x**
valid while 2θ lies in [−π/2, π/2], that is **|x| ≤ 1**.
**Step 3 — differentiate**, using d(tan⁻¹x)/dx = 1/(1 + x²):
**f′(x) = 2/(1 + x²)**
**Step 4 — evaluate at x = 1/2.**
f′(1/2) = 2/(1 + 1/4)
= 2/(5/4)
= 2 × 4/5
= **8/5** ✓
**Check the branch.** x = 1/2 satisfies |x| ≤ 1 ✓ so the simplification f = 2 tan⁻¹x
holds there and the derivative is **+**2/(1 + x²). (For |x| > 1 the identity becomes
π − 2tan⁻¹x or −π − 2tan⁻¹x, and the derivative flips sign to −2/(1 + x²) — which is why
checking the range matters.)
**Confirming by the chain rule, without the substitution.** With u = 2x/(1 + x²),
du/dx = [2(1 + x²) − 2x(2x)]/(1 + x²)² = (2 − 2x²)/(1 + x²)²
and 1 − u² = 1 − 4x²/(1 + x²)² = (1 − x²)²/(1 + x²)², so √(1 − u²) = (1 − x²)/(1 + x²) for
|x| < 1. Then
f′ = (1/√(1 − u²)) du/dx = [(1 + x²)/(1 − x²)] × 2(1 − x²)/(1 + x²)² = **2/(1 + x²)** ✓
the same, after a great deal more work — which is the point of recognising the pattern.

sin⁻¹[2x/(1 + x²)] = **2 tan⁻¹x**
cos⁻¹[(1 − x²)/(1 + x²)] = **2 tan⁻¹x**
tan⁻¹[2x/(1 − x²)] = **2 tan⁻¹x**
All three differentiate to 2/(1 + x²).
∴ 8/5.

The limits **−2 and 2** are symmetric about the origin, so the quickest way to make the
integral vanish is to choose an **odd** function.
**The rule.** For an odd function, f(−x) = −f(x), and
**∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0**
because the signed area to the left of the origin exactly cancels that to the right.
**Testing option (1): f(x) = log[(2 + x)/(2 − x)].**
f(−x) = log[(2 − x)/(2 + x)]
= log[(2 + x)/(2 − x)]⁻¹
= −log[(2 + x)/(2 − x)]
= **−f(x)** ✓ **odd**
So ∫₋₂² f(x) dx = **0** ✓ This is the answer.
(Its domain is −2 < x < 2, exactly the open interval of integration, which is consistent.)
**Testing option (2): f(x) = sin(2 + x).**
f(−x) = sin(2 − x), which is neither sin(2 + x) nor its negative ✗ **neither odd nor even**
Computing directly:
∫₋₂² sin(2 + x)dx = [−cos(2 + x)]₋₂² = −cos 4 + cos 0 = 1 − cos 4 ≈ **1·65** ≠ 0 ✗
**Testing option (3): f(x) = 2x³ + 2x + 1.**
The terms 2x³ and 2x are odd and integrate to 0, but the constant **1** does not:
∫₋₂² 1 dx = **4**
so the integral is 4 ≠ 0 ✗ A single constant term is enough to destroy the oddness.
**Testing option (4): f(x) = 2x tan x.**
Both 2x and tan x are odd, and a product of two odd functions is **even**, so this does
not vanish by symmetry. Worse, tan x has **infinite discontinuities** at ±π/2 ≈ ±1·571,
both inside [−2, 2], so the integral does not even converge ✗
**Step — conclude.** Only the first function is odd, and only its integral is zero ✓
**The rule to carry.**
**odd** function over symmetric limits → integral is **0**
**even** function over symmetric limits → integral is **2∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx**
And the quick test for the logarithm: log of a quotient is odd whenever **swapping x
for −x inverts the fraction**, which is exactly what (2 + x)/(2 − x) does.
∴ log[(2 + x)/(2 − x)].

Two binomial coefficients from the same row are equal exactly when their lower indices are
**equal or complementary**.
**Step 1 — write the two coefficients.** In (1 + x)¹⁵,
coefficient of xʳ = **¹⁵C_r**
coefficient of x^(r+3) = **¹⁵C_(r+3)**
**Step 2 — set them equal.**
¹⁵C_r = ¹⁵C_(r+3)
**Step 3 — use the symmetry property.** Since ⁿC_a = ⁿC_b requires **a = b** or
**a + b = n**, and here a = r cannot equal b = r + 3, the only possibility is
r + (r + 3) = 15
2r + 3 = 15
2r = 12
**r = 6** ✓
**Check.** The two coefficients are ¹⁵C₆ and ¹⁵C₉, and
¹⁵C₉ = ¹⁵C₍₁₅₋₉₎ = **¹⁵C₆** ✓ equal, as required. Their common value is 5005.
**Why the symmetry holds.** ⁿC_r = n!/[r!(n − r)!] is unchanged when r is replaced by
n − r, because the two factorials in the denominator simply swap places. Geometrically,
choosing r objects from n is the same as choosing which n − r to **leave out**.
**The picture.** Row 15 of Pascal's triangle is symmetric about its middle, which sits
between the 7th and 8th entries (r = 7 and r = 8, since 15 is odd). Entries equidistant
from that centre are equal, and r = 6 and r = 9 are each **1·5 positions** from it ✓
**Testing the other options quickly**, using a + b = 15:
r = 4 would pair with 11, but r + 3 = 7 ≠ 11 ✗
r = 8 would pair with 7, but r + 3 = 11 ≠ 7 ✗
r = 7 would pair with 8, but r + 3 = 10 ≠ 8 ✗
Only r = 6 pairs with r + 3 = 9 ✓
**The general result.** If the coefficients of xʳ and x^(r+k) in (1 + x)ⁿ are equal, then
2r + k = n, so **r = (n − k)/2** — here (15 − 3)/2 = **6** ✓ in one line.
∴ 6.

Write all three quantities in terms of y and the gradient, and the pattern becomes
obvious.
**Step 1 — recall the three definitions.** At a point on a curve where the ordinate is y
and the gradient is y′ = dy/dx:
**sub-tangent = y/y′**
**ordinate = y**
**sub-normal = y y′**
**Step 2 — form the ratios of consecutive terms.**
second ÷ first = y ÷ (y/y′) = y × y′/y = **y′**
third ÷ second = (y y′) ÷ y = **y′**
The two ratios are **equal** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** Three quantities with a constant ratio between consecutive terms
form a **geometric progression** ✓
So the sub-tangent, ordinate and sub-normal are in **G.P.**, with common ratio **y′**.
**The same thing seen through the G.P. test.** Three numbers p, q, r are in G.P. exactly
when **q² = pr**. Here
q² = y²
pr = (y/y′)(y y′) = **y²** ✓ equal, confirming the progression.
Notice how cleanly y′ cancels in the product — which is why the ordinate is precisely the
**geometric mean** of the other two.
**Where the definitions come from.** At the point P(x, y) on a curve, let the tangent and
normal meet the x-axis at T and N, and let M be the foot of the ordinate. Then
**sub-tangent TM = y/y′** and **sub-normal MN = y y′**, both read off from the two
right triangles PTM and PMN, which share the height y = PM.
**A worked example.** For y = x² at x = 2: y = 4 and y′ = 4.
sub-tangent = 4/4 = **1**, ordinate = **4**, sub-normal = 4 × 4 = **16**
and 1, 4, 16 is a G.P. with ratio 4 ✓ while 4 − 1 = 3 but 16 − 4 = 12, so it is certainly
not an A.P. ✗
**Why not H.P.** Their reciprocals are y′/y, 1/y, 1/(y y′), whose consecutive differences
are not equal in general — the example gives 1, 1/4, 1/16, itself a G.P. rather than an
A.P. ✗
∴ G.P.

sum: **a/(1 − r) = 4**
second term: **ar = 3/4**

**a = 4(1 − r)**
**Step 3 — substitute into the second.**
4(1 − r)r = 3/4
16r(1 − r) = 3
16r − 16r² = 3
**16r² − 16r + 3 = 0**
**Step 4 — solve the quadratic.** Factorising, since 16 × 3 = 48 and −12 − 4 = −16:
16r² − 12r − 4r + 3 = 0
4r(4r − 3) − 1(4r − 3) = 0
**(4r − 3)(4r − 1) = 0**
so **r = 3/4** or **r = 1/4**
**Step 5 — find the matching a for each.**
r = 1/4 ⟹ a = 4(1 − 1/4) = 4(3/4) = **3**
r = 3/4 ⟹ a = 4(1 − 3/4) = 4(1/4) = **1**
Both pairs are mathematically valid, but only **(a = 3, r = 1/4)** appears among the
options ✓
**Checking it.**
sum = 3/(1 − 1/4) = 3/(3/4) = 3 × 4/3 = **4** ✓
second term = 3 × 1/4 = **3/4** ✓
Both conditions met.
**Testing the other options.**
**a = 4/7, r = 3/7:** sum = (4/7)/(4/7) = 1 ≠ 4 ✗
**a = 2, r = 3/8:** sum = 2/(5/8) = 3·2 ≠ 4 ✗
**a = 3/2, r = 1/2:** sum = (3/2)/(1/2) = 3 ≠ 4 ✗
Substituting each candidate into **a/(1 − r) = 4** is in fact the quickest route under

The elements common to A × B and B × A are the **ordered pairs** lying in both, and they
are exactly the pairs built from A ∩ B.
**Step 1 — characterise a common element.** An ordered pair (x, y) belongs to
**A × B** when x ∈ A and y ∈ B
**B × A** when x ∈ B and y ∈ A
For it to be in both, x must lie in **A and B**, and y must lie in **A and B** too:
x ∈ A ∩ B and y ∈ A ∩ B
**Step 2 — write the intersection as a product.**
**(A × B) ∩ (B × A) = (A ∩ B) × (A ∩ B)**
**Step 3 — count.** If |A ∩ B| = n, then the number of ordered pairs with both entries
drawn from that set is
n × n = **n²** ✓
**A concrete check.** Take A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}, so A ∩ B = {2, 3} and
**n = 2**.
A × B = {(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),(2,2),(2,3),(2,4),(3,2),(3,3),(3,4)}
B × A = {(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,2),(3,3),(4,1),(4,2),(4,3)}
The pairs appearing in **both** are
(2,2), (2,3), (3,2), (3,3) — exactly **4 = n²** ✓
and they are precisely the pairs from {2, 3} × {2, 3} ✓
**Why not n.** Counting only the "diagonal" pairs (x, x) with x ∈ A ∩ B gives n, missing
the mixed pairs like (2, 3) and (3, 2). Both entries range **independently** over A ∩ B,
so the count multiplies rather than merely matching.
**Why not 2n.** That would be the size of a **union** of two sets of size n, not a
Cartesian product.
**Why not 0.** Unless A and B are disjoint (n = 0), there are always common pairs — at the
very least (x, x) for each x in A ∩ B.
**The general rule.** |A × B| = |A| × |B| for any sets, and here both factors are
|A ∩ B| = n ✓
∴ n².

The **coefficient of variation** measures the spread as a **percentage of the mean**:
**CV = (σ / x̄) × 100**
**Step 1 — substitute.** With CV = 60 and σ = 24:
60 = (24/x̄) × 100
**Step 2 — rearrange.**
60 x̄ = 2400
**x̄ = 2400/60 = 40** ✓
**Check.** CV = (24/40) × 100 = 0·6 × 100 = **60** ✓ as given.
**The rearranged formula**, worth having ready:
**x̄ = 100σ/CV**
= 100 × 24/60 = 2400/60 = **40** ✓ in one step.
**Why CV exists.** The standard deviation alone cannot say whether a distribution is
widely spread, because it carries the data's **units**: σ = 24 is enormous for exam marks
out of 50 but trivial for annual incomes. Dividing by the mean strips the units away, so
the CV is a **pure number** and two distributions measured in different units can be
compared directly.
**Reading the answer.** A CV of 60% with x̄ = 40 means the typical deviation from the
average, 24, is more than half the average itself — a markedly scattered distribution.
**Why the small options are impossible.** **7/20 = 0·35** and **1/40 = 0·025** are both far
**smaller** than σ = 24. A mean smaller than the standard deviation would give a CV of
several thousand per cent, not 60 ✗ Since CV = 60 < 100, the formula forces σ < x̄, so the
mean **must exceed 24** — and only 40 does. That observation alone picks the answer.
**And 20/7 ≈ 2·86** fails the same test ✗
**A caution about the factor 100.** Leaving it out gives x̄ = 24/60 = 0·4, a hundredfold
error. The coefficient of variation is quoted as a **percentage**, so the 100 is part of
the definition.
∴ 40.

the right. (Directly: [x⁴/4]₋₂² = 4 − 4 = 0 ✓)
**x is odd**, so ∫₋₂² x dx = **0**. (Directly: [x²/2]₋₂² = 2 − 2 = 0 ✓)
**1 is even**, so ∫₋₂² 1 dx = [x]₋₂² = 2 − (−2) = **4**
**Step 3 — add.**
= a(0) + b(0) + c(4) = **4c** ✓
So the value depends **only on c** ✓
**Why a and b drop out.** Both ax³ and bx are **odd** functions, and the integral of an
odd function over limits symmetric about 0 is always zero — however large the coefficients
are. The constant term c is the only **even** part of the integrand, so it alone
contributes.
**A numerical check.** Take a = 100, b = −50, c = 1:
∫₋₂²(100x³ − 50x + 1)dx = 100[x⁴/4]₋₂² − 50[x²/2]₋₂² + [x]₋₂²
= 100(4 − 4) − 50(2 − 2) + (2 + 2)

**value of b** ✗ — bx is odd and integrates to 0.
**value of a** ✗ — ax³ is odd likewise.
**values of a and b** ✗ — neither contributes.
**The rule to carry.** Over symmetric limits [−L, L]:
**odd** terms (x, x³, x⁵, sin x, …) contribute **nothing**
**even** terms (1, x², x⁴, cos x, …) contribute **twice** the half-integral
So in a question of this shape, simply strike out every odd power and integrate what
remains.
∴ value of c.
